annotations.title: Vitamin B12 - Health Professional Fact Sheet

content.text:
For **vitamin B12, there isn’t an official “too much” upper limit** for healthy adults. The NIH says no Tolerable Upper Intake Level has been set because B12 has **low toxicity**, and high doses are generally considered safe. ([ods.od.nih.gov](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/VitaminB12-HealthProfessional/?uid=c273e26eea9a1s16&utm_source=openai))

That said:

- **Daily need is small:** adults need about **2.4 mcg/day**.
- Many supplements contain **500–5,000 mcg**, which is far above the daily requirement but usually not dangerous because absorption is limited and excess is excreted.
- **Common medical doses** for deficiency are often **1,000 mcg/day orally** or periodic injections, depending on the cause.

**When it may be “too much” practically:**  
If you’re taking high-dose B12 **without a deficiency or medical reason**, it’s probably unnecessary. Mayo Clinic notes high doses can sometimes cause side effects such as **headache, nausea/vomiting, diarrhea, fatigue/weakness, or tingling sensations**. ([mayoclinic.org](https://www.mayoclinic.org/drugs-supplements-vitamin-b12/art-20363663?p=1&utm_source=openai))

**Also important:** a **high B12 blood level** isn’t always from supplements; it can sometimes be associated with liver disease, kidney disease, blood disorders, or other conditions, so it’s worth discussing with a clinician if your lab result is unexpectedly high. Cleveland Clinic notes “high B12” means your blood level is above expected, and it generally takes extremely high doses to cause toxic effects. ([my.clevelandclinic.org](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/high-b12-levels?utm_source=openai))

**Rule of thumb:**  
- If you’re supplementing casually, **25–100 mcg/day** is more than enough for many people.  
- If you’re vegan/vegetarian, older, on metformin or acid-reducing meds, or have low B12, higher doses may be appropriate.  
- If you’re taking **1,000+ mcg daily long-term**, it’s usually safe but worth checking whether you actually need it.
